metadata.file_name: 89. Lee et al. (2025). Uncovering Behavioral Patterns in Creative Thinking: Utilizing and Interpreting PISA 2022 Process Data.pdf
metadata.title: Uncovering Behavioral Patterns in Creative Thinking: Utilizing and Interpreting PISA 2022 Process Data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This article is a review/theory-oriented synthesis of how PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (CT) process data can be used, rather than an empirical re-analysis with a reported analytic sample. As such, it does not specify whether student-level sampling/survey weights or replicate weights were applied, nor does it name any weight variables from the OECD PISA database. For researchers using PISA 2022 CT process data in their own analyses, the OECD PISA microdata are typically designed for complex survey inference; analysts should therefore use the provided sampling weights (and replicate weights if available) when estimating population-representative statistics. The paper also notes that process data are nested within units and that official PISA analyses use specific engagement indicators derived from response-time metrics, which should guide how weighting and scaling are handled in downstream modeling.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper does not conduct an empirical student-level predictive analysis with a cognitive achievement outcome that would require Plausible Values (PVs). Instead, it describes available PISA 2022 CT process metrics (e.g., response time, actions, visits) and discusses modeling approaches conceptually, including how process data could be integrated with item responses. Because no PV-based dependent variable is modeled in the paper’s own analysis, PV handling is not applicable; additionally, the paper does not report a missing-data strategy for an empirical model, so missing-data handling is not reported.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: No analytic subsample is defined because the article does not report an original empirical dataset analysis. It provides an illustrative descriptive example using released PISA 2022 CT items (Robot Story and Save the River) and reports process-metric ranges sourced from the OECD codebook for participating countries, but it does not specify an analytic sample construction pipeline (e.g., country list, grade restrictions, item/unit inclusion rules, or missing-data exclusions) for a fitted model.

data.outcome_summary: This article is not an empirical predictive study; it is a review/synthesis explaining what PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (CT) process data are and how they can be analyzed to study cognitive and affective dynamics in creative ideation. It describes five process metrics available from PISA 2022 CT log files—total time on item, time to first action, number of actions, number of visits, and number of short visits—and notes that official PISA engagement indicators use response-time-based metrics while other measures are typically reserved for exploratory research. The paper also outlines model-based approaches (data mining and mixture/IRT-based ideas) and provides an illustrative descriptive example for two released items (Robot Story and Save the River) using codebook-derived ranges rather than fitting a predictive model. Because no ML model is trained and no PV-based outcome is estimated in the paper itself, there are no reported predictive performance metrics; the main contribution is methodological guidance and interpretation cautions (e.g., construct alignment, disengagement definitions, and nested dependencies).
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction sets main_findings to an empty array and leaves ML technique fields empty because the manuscript does not report an original empirical ML pipeline with a defined target variable, fitted model, and performance metrics. Instead, it reviews PISA 2022 CT process data types and discusses potential analytical strategies, with only a descriptive illustrative example based on released items/codebook ranges. Consequently, there is no country-level analytic sample definition, no PV handling procedure for an estimated achievement outcome, and no missing-data handling strategy for a fitted model.
